Anyone who is a bird enthusiast knows about the blight of house sparrows - these dangerous little cunts that have spread to every continent except Antarctica and exist basically everywhere people do. Now, it wouldn't be that bad if they were docile, but they are super aggressive and will maim and kill native bird species, and are effectively dis-placing many hundreds if not thousands of native species.

You can find lots of detailed articles on how they are an invasive species, but let me share an anecdote I just experienced with them:

I was going into a grocery store when I noticed someone had pulled a house sparrow nest out of a crevice, leaving two nestlings laying on the ground. Even though I hate the species, I couldn't stand to see two individuals die like that, and I wanted to expand my bird collection anyway - perhaps there is some good breeding potential with wild house sparrows - so I decided to take them in and raise them. That was two weeks ago, and now the oldest sparrow is fully feathered and starting its first attempts at flight, so I decided it was a good time to try introducing it to my other birds - 3 wild finches who were also rescues from a nest crows had gotten into a month and a half ago.

These three three are fledged, independent, and basically adults now, but as soon as I put the sparrow in the cage, it began snapping at them. Given their nature, I wasn't wholly surprised, but I was astonished that it was aggressive this early in its life - I had assumed a lot of the aggression would come later in its life once it was ready to start breeding, but no. Just to confirm that it wasn't afraid of the finches, I sat it on the far side of the perch from the finches, and this little asshole, who is still so weak it could barely stay balanced on the perch, proceeded to scoot down the entire length of the perch to get within pecking range of the finches, who seemed bewildered that I would put something so aggressive in with them.

So I took the sparrow out and, out of curiosity, returned with the other chick which is still a nestling with pinfeathers. Holding it in the palm of my hand, I lifted it to the finches, and this cunt, who can't even manage to stand yet, begins snapping and pecking at the finches as well. That surprised me.

Neither of these birds have ever seen an adult bird of any kind before - their eyes were closed when I found them. I must say that I am impressed at their genetic memory of what non-sparrows look like, but needless to say, any notions of caging them together have gone out the window.
